topics.name: Mechanics
concepts: Dimensions: angular momentum and h [ML²T⁻¹]; viscosity η [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]; work, torque [ML²T⁻²] [repeat]
Error in Z = AᵃBᵇ: ΔZ/Z = a ΔA/A + b ΔB/B; g = 4π²L/T² gives ΔL/L + 2ΔT/T
Candela is the SI base unit of luminous intensity; lumen = flux, lux = illuminance [repeat]
Round trip at v₁ and v₂: average speed 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂) [repeat]
Projectile: R = u²sin2θ/g; KE at top = K cos²θ (θ from horizontal) [repeat]
Equal KE: p = √(2mK) ∝ √m; impulse = Δp; equal masses in elastic head-on collision swap velocities [repeat]
Limiting friction μN; angle of repose tanθ = μ
Torque produces angular acceleration: τ = Iα; P = τω; no torque → Iω constant [repeat]
Rod: I = ML²/12 about centre, ML²/3 about end; K = L/√12 about centre
Floating at interface: ρ = sum of (fraction × liquid density); stable ship needs metacentre above CG [repeat]
Heating: liquid viscosity falls, gas viscosity rises; Young's modulus falls [repeat]
Water–glass angle of contact acute → concave meniscus, rise h = 2T cosθ/(rρg); mercury convex [repeat]
Stokes F = 6πηrv; Poiseuille Q ∝ r⁴; Bernoulli ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²)
Vertical circle: v_top ≥ √(gr), v_bottom ≥ √(5gr); SHM v_max = Aω at mean position
Escape velocity √(2gR) = 11.2 km/s, independent of body's mass, ∝ R at fixed density; g_h ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) [repeat]
Y = FL/(AΔL); energy density ½ stress × strain; Poisson's ratio = lateral/longitudinal strain

topics.name: Heat and thermodynamics
concepts: Zeroth law defines temperature; F = 9C/5 + 32, a 1°C difference = 1.8°F = 1 K
Stefan–Boltzmann E = σT⁴: doubling T gives 16× radiation [repeat]
Pyrometer for furnaces; mercury freezes at −39°C; platinum thermometer uses R = R₀(1 + αθ)
Conduction H = KAΔθ/L; Sun's heat reaches Earth by radiation
α : β : γ = 1 : 2 : 3; a hole in a heated plate grows; γ_real = γ_apparent + γ_vessel
Heating a liquid with an immersed solid: upthrust falls (liquid expands more), apparent weight rises [repeat]
Water densest at 4°C; triple point 273.16 K
Q = mcΔθ, Q = mL; ice L = 336 J/g; steam burns worse (latent heat)
Mixture: heat lost = heat gained; check if all ice melts before finding final temperature
Kinetic theory P = ⅓ρc²; mean KE per molecule (3/2)kT, same for all gases at same T
v_rms = √(3RT/M) ∝ √(T/M): H₂ is 4× faster than O₂
First law Q = ΔU + W; isochoric W = 0; cyclic ΔU = 0; Cp − Cv = R
Adiabatic PV^γ = constant, Q = 0, gas cools on expansion; adiabatic slope = γ × isothermal
Carnot η = 1 − T₂/T₁; refrigerator COP = T₂/(T₁ − T₂)
Entropy ΔS = Q/T (kelvin); isolated irreversible process: entropy increases; Kelvin–Planck forbids 100% engines

concepts: v = fλ; sound in solids > liquids > gases; none in vacuum
Laplace: v = √(γP/ρ) (adiabatic); v ∝ √T, independent of pressure
Phase difference = (2π/λ) × path difference
Nodes λ/2 apart; closed pipe v/4L odd harmonics only; open pipe v/2L all harmonics
String: v = √(T/μ), n loops have n + 1 nodes
Doppler f' = f(v ± v₀)/(v ∓ vₛ); echo from cliff: f(v + u)/(v − u) [repeat]
Pitch ↔ frequency, loudness ↔ amplitude, quality ↔ overtones; +10 dB = 10× intensity
Intensity ∝ amplitude²; I_max/I_min = (a₁ + a₂)²/(a₁ − a₂)² [repeat]
Mirror 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; convex mirror image always virtual, erect, diminished
Apparent depth = real depth/n; layers add: Σ t/n [repeat]
n depends on wavelength, material, temperature, not on angle of incidence; frequency never changes on refraction [repeat]
Lens maker 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂): equiconvex R = 20 cm, n = 1.5 → +5 D [repeat]
Dispersive power ω = (n_v − n_r)/(n_y − 1); achromat ω₁/f₁ + ω₂/f₂ = 0
YDSE β = λD/d; in a medium β/n; dark fringe at odd multiples of λ/2
Single slit first minimum a sinθ = λ; grating d sinθ = nλ; resolving power ∝ D/λ
Polaroid passes I₀/2 of unpolarised light; Malus I = I₀cos²θ; Brewster tan θp = n, rays at 90°

questions.q: The dimensional formula of Planck's constant is
questions.x: h = E/ν = [ML²T⁻²]/[T⁻¹] = [ML²T⁻¹], the same as angular momentum.
questions.trap: [ML²T⁻²] is energy; students forget to divide by frequency.

questions.q: Which pair of quantities has the same dimensions?
questions.x: Both are force × distance, [ML²T⁻²]. Impulse is [MLT⁻¹] while force is [MLT⁻²]; strain is dimensionless.

questions.q: The radius of a sphere is measured with a 2% error. The maximum percentage error in its volume is
questions.trap: 8% comes from cubing 2; the error is multiplied by the power.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m/s. Its maximum height is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.trap: 40 m comes from forgetting the 2 in u²/2g.

questions.q: For the same launch speed, a projectile fired at 30° has the same horizontal range as one fired at
questions.x: R = u²sin2θ/g and sin60° = sin120°, so angles θ and 90° − θ give equal ranges.

questions.q: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes uniformly and stops in 4 s. The distance covered while braking is
questions.trap: 80 m uses s = ut, ignoring the deceleration.

questions.q: Newton's first law of motion gives the concept of
questions.x: A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an external force acts on it; this property is inertia.

questions.q: A 50 kg person stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s². The scale reads (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.x: Apparent weight R = m(g + a) = 50 × 12 = 600 N.
questions.trap: 400 N is the reading for downward acceleration.

questions.q: A 4 kg gun fires a 20 g bullet at 500 m/s. The recoil speed of the gun is
questions.x: Momentum conservation: 4 × v = 0.02 × 500 = 10, so v = 2.5 m/s.
questions.trap: 25 m/s comes from writing 20 g as 0.2 kg.

questions.q: If the linear momentum of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes
questions.x: KE = p²/2m, so KE ∝ p²; doubling p gives 4 times the KE.

questions.q: A pump lifts 100 kg of water through a height of 10 m in 20 s. Its power is (g = 10 m/s²)
The maximum safe speed of a car on an unbanked circular road of radius 40 m with friction coefficient 0.25 is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.x: Friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r, so v = √(μrg) = √(0.25 × 40 × 10) = √100 = 10 m/s.
questions.trap: 100 m/s comes from forgetting the square root.

questions.q: The escape velocity from the Earth's surface is about
questions.x: vₑ = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s. 7.9 km/s is the orbital speed of a satellite near the surface; vₑ = √2 × orbital speed.
questions.trap: 7.9 km/s is orbital velocity, not escape velocity.

questions.q: At a height equal to the Earth's radius above its surface, the acceleration due to gravity becomes
questions.x: g' = gR²/(R + h)² = gR²/(2R)² = g/4.
questions.trap: g/2 assumes g falls linearly with height.

questions.q: If the orbital radius of a planet around the Sun becomes 4 times, its period of revolution becomes
questions.x: Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2) = 4^(3/2) = 8.
questions.trap: 16 times comes from squaring instead of using the 3/2 power.

questions.q: A spinning skater pulls in her arms so that her moment of inertia is halved. Her rotational kinetic energy
questions.x: No external torque, so L = Iω is constant. KE = L²/2I, so halving I doubles the KE (the extra energy comes from her muscles).
questions.trap: 'Same': confusing conservation of angular momentum with conservation of KE.

questions.q: For a solid sphere (I = ⅖mR²) rolling without slipping, the fraction of its total kinetic energy that is rotational is
questions.x: KE_rot = ½(⅖mR²)ω² = mv²/5; total = mv²/2 + mv²/5 = 7mv²/10; fraction = (1/5)/(7/10) = 2/7.
questions.trap: 5/7 is the translational fraction; 2/5 is from I = ⅖mR².

questions.q: The Young's modulus of a perfectly rigid body is
questions.x: Y = stress/strain. A perfectly rigid body has zero strain under any stress, so Y is infinite.
questions.trap: Zero: students link 'no deformation' with a zero modulus.

questions.q: A wire stretches by 1 mm under a load. A wire of the same material, twice as long and of twice the radius, under the same load stretches by
questions.x: ΔL = FL/(πr²Y). L doubles (×2) and r² becomes 4 times (÷4): ΔL = 1 × 2/4 = 0.5 mm.

questions.q: Bernoulli's theorem is based on the conservation of
questions.x: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant: pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume add to a constant.
questions.trap: Mass is the basis of the equation of continuity, not Bernoulli.

questions.q: Water flows at 2 m/s through a pipe of cross-section 4 cm². Where the cross-section narrows to 1 cm², its speed is
questions.x: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ → 4 × 2 = 1 × v₂, so v₂ = 8 m/s.

questions.q: A small steel ball falls through glycerine with terminal velocity v. A ball of the same material with twice the radius has terminal velocity
questions.x: Stokes' law gives v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η, so v_t ∝ r²; doubling r gives 4v.

questions.q: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius r and surface tension T is
questions.x: A soap bubble has two free surfaces, so excess pressure = 2 × 2T/r = 4T/r.
questions.trap: 2T/r is for a liquid drop, which has only one surface.

questions.q: The temperature at which the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales give the same reading is
If α is the coefficient of linear expansion of a solid, its coefficient of cubical expansion is
questions.x: α : β : γ = 1 : 2 : 3, so γ = 3α (β = 2α is the areal coefficient).

questions.q: 200 g of water at 80°C is mixed with 100 g of water at 20°C. Neglecting heat loss, the final temperature is
questions.trap: 50°C is the simple average, ignoring the unequal masses.

questions.q: The heat needed to melt 10 g of ice at 0°C into water at 0°C is (latent heat of fusion = 336 J/g)
questions.x: Q = mL = 10 × 336 = 3360 J; temperature stays constant during melting.

questions.q: If the absolute temperature of a gas becomes 4 times, the rms speed of its molecules becomes
questions.x: v_rms = √(3RT/M), so v_rms ∝ √T; √4 = 2.

questions.q: A gas at 27°C is heated at constant pressure until its volume doubles. Its final temperature is
questions.x: Charles' law V ∝ T in kelvin: T₂ = 2 × 300 K = 600 K = 327°C.
questions.trap: 54°C doubles the Celsius value; gas laws need kelvin.

questions.q: The ratio of specific heats γ = Cp/Cv for a monatomic ideal gas is
questions.x: Monatomic: Cv = 3R/2, Cp = 5R/2, so γ = 5/3. A diatomic gas has 7/5.
questions.trap: 7/5 is for a diatomic gas.

questions.q: In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, which quantity is zero?
questions.x: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. T constant ⇒ ΔU = 0, so heat absorbed equals work done.

questions.q: A Carnot engine works between 527°C and 127°C. Its efficiency is
questions.x: Use kelvin: T₁ = 800 K, T₂ = 400 K. η = 1 − T₂/T₁ = 1 − 400/800 = 50%.
questions.trap: 76% comes from 1 − 127/527, using Celsius.

questions.q: If the absolute temperature of a black body is doubled, the total power it radiates becomes
questions.x: Stefan–Boltzmann law: E = σT⁴, so 2⁴ = 16 times.

questions.q: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration of the particle is maximum at
questions.x: a = −ω²x, so |a| is largest where |x| is largest, at the extremes. Velocity is maximum at the mean position.
questions.trap: Mean position: that is where velocity, not acceleration, is maximum.

questions.q: If the length of a simple pendulum is increased to 4 times, its time period becomes
If the amplitude of a simple harmonic oscillator is doubled, its total energy becomes
questions.x: E = ½mω²A², so E ∝ A²; doubling A gives 4 times the energy.

questions.q: Sound waves in air are
questions.x: Air particles vibrate along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions. Gases cannot support transverse waves.

questions.q: The fundamental frequency of an 85 cm long pipe closed at one end is (speed of sound = 340 m/s)
questions.x: Closed pipe: L = λ/4, so f = v/4L = 340/(4 × 0.85) = 100 Hz.
questions.trap: 200 Hz uses the open-pipe formula v/2L.

questions.q: Two tuning forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. The number of beats heard per second is
questions.x: Beat frequency = |f₁ − f₂| = 260 − 256 = 4 per second.

questions.q: A source of frequency 500 Hz moves towards a stationary observer at 30 m/s. If the speed of sound is 330 m/s, the observed frequency is
questions.x: Source approaching: f' = f·v/(v − vₛ) = 500 × 330/300 = 550 Hz.
questions.trap: 545 Hz uses the moving-observer formula f(v + v₀)/v.

questions.q: The tension in a stretched string is increased by 44%, with length and mass unchanged. Its fundamental frequency increases by
questions.x: f ∝ √T. New f = √1.44 × f = 1.2f, an increase of 20%.
questions.trap: 22% halves 44%, treating the square root as a simple halving.

questions.q: An object is placed at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. Its image is
o: Real, inverted, same size, at the centre of curvature
Virtual, erect, magnified, behind the mirror
Real, inverted, diminished, at the focus
Real, inverted, magnified, beyond the centre of curvature
questions.x: With u = 2f the mirror formula gives v = 2f and magnification −1: a real, inverted, same-size image at C.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. The image is formed
o: 12 cm from the lens, on the other side
60 cm from the lens, on the same side
10 cm from the lens, on the other side
60 cm from the lens, on the other side
questions.x: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f with u = −30: 1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so v = +60 cm, a real image on the other side.
questions.trap: 12 cm comes from adding 1/20 + 1/30 with a wrong sign.

questions.q: The power of a convex lens of focal length 50 cm is
questions.x: P = 1/f (metres) = 1/0.5 = +2 D; positive for a converging lens.
questions.trap: +0.5 D forgets that power is the reciprocal of f in metres.

questions.q: The critical angle for light going from a medium of refractive index √2 into air is
When white light passes through a glass prism, the colour deviated the most is
questions.x: Refractive index of glass is largest for the shortest wavelength (violet), so violet deviates most and red least.

questions.q: In Young's double-slit experiment, λ = 600 nm, slit separation = 1 mm and slit–screen distance = 1 m. The fringe width is
The phenomenon that shows light waves are transverse is
questions.x: Only transverse waves can be polarised. Interference and diffraction also occur with longitudinal waves such as sound.

questions.q: Light falls on glass of refractive index √3 at the polarising (Brewster) angle. The angle of incidence is
questions.x: Brewster's law: tan θp = μ = √3, so θp = 60°.

questions.q: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm is placed in contact with a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. The combination behaves as a
o: Convex lens of focal length 20 cm
Concave lens of focal length 20 cm
Convex lens of focal length 30 cm
Convex lens of focal length 6.7 cm
questions.trap: 6.7 cm treats both lenses as positive, ignoring the concave sign.

questions.q: The SI unit of luminous intensity is
questions.x: The candela (cd) is one of the seven SI base units. Lumen is the unit of luminous flux and lux of illuminance.
questions.trap: Lumen: it measures luminous flux, not intensity.

questions.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.x: Potential (work per unit charge) has magnitude only. Field, momentum and torque all have direction.
questions.trap: Electric field and potential are confused because both describe the same charge.

questions.q: The dimensional formula of the coefficient of viscosity is
questions.x: F = ηA(dv/dx), so η = F/(A·dv/dx) = [MLT⁻²]/([L²][T⁻¹]) = [ML⁻¹T⁻¹].
questions.trap: [ML⁻¹T⁻²] is pressure/stress; students forget the velocity gradient.

questions.q: The length of a simple pendulum is measured with a 2% error and its period with a 1% error. The maximum percentage error in g is
questions.x: g = 4π²L/T², so Δg/g = ΔL/L + 2ΔT/T = 2% + 2 × 1% = 4%.
questions.trap: 3%: adding the errors without doubling the error in T.

questions.q: The number of significant figures in 0.05020 is
questions.x: Leading zeros do not count; the digits 5, 0, 2 and the trailing 0 after the decimal point do: 4 significant figures.
questions.trap: 3: dropping the trailing zero, which is significant after a decimal point.

questions.q: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at a point at right angles to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is
questions.trap: 7 N: adding magnitudes as if the forces were parallel.

questions.q: The angle between the vectors A = î + ĵ and B = î − ĵ is
questions.x: A·B = (1)(1) + (1)(−1) = 0, so the vectors are perpendicular.

questions.q: A man drives to work at 60 km/h and returns along the same road at 40 km/h. His average speed for the round trip is
questions.x: Equal distances: v_avg = 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂) = 2 × 60 × 40/100 = 48 km/h.
questions.trap: 50 km/h: taking the simple mean, but more time is spent at the slower speed.

questions.q: A projectile is launched at 45° to the horizontal with kinetic energy K. Its kinetic energy at the highest point is
questions.x: At the top only the horizontal velocity u cos45° remains: KE = K cos²45° = K/2.
questions.trap: Zero: forgetting the horizontal velocity does not vanish at the top.

questions.q: A ball is thrown with kinetic energy E in a direction making 30° with the vertical. Its kinetic energy at the highest point is
questions.x: Angle with the horizontal = 60°. At the top KE = E cos²60° = E/4.
questions.trap: 3E/4: using cos²30° with the angle measured from the vertical.

questions.q: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives
questions.x: Slope = Δv/Δt = acceleration. The area under the v–t graph gives displacement.
questions.trap: Displacement: that is the area under the graph, not its slope.

questions.q: A stone dropped from rest falls freely. The distances it covers in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds are in the ratio
questions.x: Distance in the nth second = g(2n − 1)/2, giving 5 m, 15 m, 25 m: ratio 1 : 3 : 5.
questions.trap: 1 : 4 : 9 is the ratio of total distances after 1, 2, 3 s.

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from the top of a 45 m high tower. It lands at a horizontal distance of (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.x: Fall time t = √(2h/g) = √9 = 3 s; horizontal distance = 10 × 3 = 30 m.

questions.q: A body falling through air reaches its terminal velocity when
o: The net force on it becomes zero
questions.x: Air resistance grows with speed until it balances weight (minus upthrust); net force and acceleration become zero, so speed stays constant.

questions.q: Two bodies of masses 4 kg and 16 kg have equal kinetic energies. The ratio of their linear momenta is
questions.x: p = √(2mK); with equal K, p ∝ √m: √4 : √16 = 1 : 2.
questions.trap: 1 : 4: taking p ∝ m and forgetting the square root.

questions.q: A 5 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor with coefficient of static friction 0.4. The least horizontal force that just starts it moving is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.x: Limiting friction = μmg = 0.4 × 5 × 10 = 20 N.

questions.q: The angle of repose θ and the coefficient of static friction μ are related by
questions.x: On the incline at repose, mg sinθ = μ mg cosθ, so μ = tan θ.

questions.q: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall normally at 10 m/s and rebounds with the same speed. The impulse on the ball is
questions.x: Impulse = Δp = m(v − (−v)) = 0.2 × 20 = 4 N s.
questions.trap: Zero: treating rebound speed as no change, but velocity reverses.

questions.q: In a perfectly elastic head-on collision, a moving ball strikes an identical ball at rest. After the collision
o: Both move together with half the initial velocity
The first ball stops and the second moves with the first ball's velocity
The first ball rebounds with the same speed and the second stays at rest
questions.x: Equal masses in an elastic head-on collision exchange velocities (momentum and KE both conserved).
questions.trap: 'Move together': that happens only in a perfectly inelastic collision.

questions.q: A 2 kg body moving at 6 m/s hits and sticks to a 4 kg body at rest. Their common velocity is
questions.x: Momentum conserved: 2 × 6 = (2 + 4)v, so v = 12/6 = 2 m/s.

questions.q: A force of 10 N moves a body 5 m along a line making 60° with the force. The work done is
questions.x: W = Fs cosθ = 10 × 5 × cos60° = 25 J.
questions.trap: 43.3 J uses sin60° instead of cos60°.

questions.q: A rigid body is in rotational equilibrium when
o: The net force on it is zero
The net torque on it about any point is zero
questions.x: Translational equilibrium needs ΣF = 0; rotational equilibrium needs Στ = 0.
questions.trap: 'Net force zero' is the condition for translational, not rotational, equilibrium.

questions.q: A net external torque acting on a rigid body produces
o: Linear acceleration of its centre only
questions.x: τ = Iα: torque is the rotational analogue of force and causes angular acceleration.
questions.trap: Uniform angular velocity needs zero net torque.

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a uniform rod of mass M and length L about a perpendicular axis through one end is
questions.x: I_centre = ML²/12; parallel-axis: I_end = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3.
questions.trap: ML²/12 is about the centre, not the end.

questions.q: The radius of gyration of a uniform rod of length L about a perpendicular axis through its centre is
questions.trap: L/√3 is about an end.

questions.q: A uniform rod of mass 3 kg and length 2 m rotates at 2 rad/s about a perpendicular axis through its centre. Its rotational kinetic energy is
questions.x: I = ML²/12 = 3 × 4/12 = 1 kg m²; KE = ½Iω² = ½ × 1 × 4 = 2 J.
questions.trap: 8 J uses I = ML²/3 (axis through an end).

questions.q: The power delivered by a torque τ to a body rotating with angular velocity ω is
questions.x: Rotational analogue of P = Fv: P = τω.

questions.q: A floating ship is in stable equilibrium when its metacentre is
questions.x: If the metacentre lies above the centre of gravity, a tilt creates a restoring couple; below it the couple overturns the ship.

questions.q: A solid cube floats at the boundary between oil (density 800 kg/m³) and water (1000 kg/m³), with half its volume in each liquid. The density of the cube is
questions.x: Weight = total upthrust: ρV g = (V/2)(800)g + (V/2)(1000)g, so ρ = 900 kg/m³.
questions.trap: 1800: adding the densities without halving.

questions.q: When the temperature rises, the viscosity of
o: Both a gas and a liquid increase
Both a gas and a liquid decrease
A gas increases and a liquid decreases
A gas decreases and a liquid increases
questions.x: Liquid viscosity falls as cohesive forces weaken; gas viscosity rises as faster molecules transfer more momentum between layers.
questions.trap: 'Both decrease': applying the liquid rule to gases.

questions.q: Water in a clean glass capillary tube forms a meniscus that is
o: Convex, because the angle of contact is obtuse
Concave, because the angle of contact is acute
Flat, because the angle of contact is 90°
Concave, because the angle of contact is obtuse
questions.x: Adhesion (water–glass) exceeds cohesion, so θ < 90°, the surface curves up at the walls (concave) and water rises. Mercury is the convex case.

questions.q: Water rises 4 cm in a capillary tube. In a tube of the same glass with half the radius, it rises
questions.x: h = 2T cosθ/(rρg) ∝ 1/r, so halving r doubles h: 8 cm.
questions.trap: 16 cm: treating h ∝ 1/r².

questions.q: By Poiseuille's equation, if the radius of a tube is doubled with the same pressure difference, the volume of liquid flowing per second becomes
questions.x: Q = πPr⁴/(8ηl) ∝ r⁴, so 2⁴ = 16 times.

questions.q: By Stokes' law, the viscous drag on a small sphere of radius r moving at speed v through a fluid of viscosity η is
questions.x: Stokes' law: F = 6πηrv (small sphere, streamline flow).

questions.q: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) flows through a horizontal pipe. Where its speed rises from 2 m/s to 4 m/s, the pressure falls by
questions.x: Bernoulli: ΔP = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = ½ × 1000 × (16 − 4) = 6000 Pa.
questions.trap: 2000 Pa uses ½ρ(v₂ − v₁)² instead of the difference of squares.

questions.q: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 2.5 m. The least speed at the top for the string to stay taut is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.x: At the top, with tension just zero, mg = mv²/r, so v = √(gr) = √25 = 5 m/s.

questions.q: The minimum speed at the lowest point for a body on a string to complete a vertical circle of radius r is
questions.x: Top needs v² = gr; energy: v_bottom² = gr + 2g(2r) = 5gr.
questions.trap: √(gr) is the minimum at the top, not the bottom.

questions.q: A particle executes SHM given by x = 0.05 sin(10t) metre. Its maximum speed is
In simple harmonic motion, the speed of the particle is maximum at
questions.x: v = ω√(A² − x²) is largest at x = 0 (mean position) and zero at the extremes.
questions.trap: Extreme positions: there acceleration, not speed, is maximum.

questions.q: If the mass hung on a spring is made four times, the period of oscillation
In forced oscillations, resonance occurs when
o: The driving frequency is twice the natural frequency
The driving frequency equals the natural frequency
questions.x: At resonance the driver matches the natural frequency, energy transfer is greatest and amplitude peaks.

questions.q: A simple pendulum has a period of 2 s on Earth. On a planet where g is one-fourth of Earth's value, its period is
questions.x: T ∝ 1/√g; g ÷ 4 gives T × 2 = 4 s.
questions.trap: 1 s: thinking a smaller g makes the pendulum faster.

questions.q: A planet has the same density as the Earth but twice its radius. The escape velocity from it is (Earth: 11.2 km/s)
questions.x: v_e = √(2GM/R) = R√(8πGρ/3) ∝ R at fixed density, so 2 × 11.2 = 22.4 km/s.
questions.trap: 15.8 km/s: taking v_e ∝ √R instead of v_e ∝ R at fixed density.

questions.q: The escape velocity of a body from the Earth does NOT depend on
questions.x: v_e = √(2GM/R): the projectile's own mass cancels.

questions.q: Taking R = 6400 km, the height above the Earth's surface at which g becomes 1% less than at the surface is about
questions.x: For h ≪ R, g_h = g(1 − 2h/R); 2h/R = 0.01 gives h = 32 km.
questions.trap: 64 km uses the depth formula g(1 − d/R).

questions.q: A satellite orbits just above the Earth's surface. To escape from the Earth, its speed must be multiplied by
questions.x: Orbital speed √(gR) and escape speed √(2gR): ratio √2.

questions.q: When a metal wire is heated, its Young's modulus
questions.x: Heating weakens interatomic forces, so the same stress produces more strain: Y falls with temperature.

questions.q: The elastic potential energy stored per unit volume of a stretched wire is
questions.x: U/V = ½ × stress × strain = ½Y(strain)².
questions.trap: stress/strain is Young's modulus, not energy density.

questions.q: Poisson's ratio is the ratio of
questions.x: σ = lateral strain/longitudinal strain; dimensionless.

questions.q: A wire 2 m long with cross-section 1 mm² stretches by 1 mm under a load of 100 N. Its Young's modulus is
questions.trap: 2 × 10⁸: converting mm² to 10⁻³ m² instead of 10⁻⁶ m².

questions.q: A metal sphere hangs fully immersed in a liquid. When the whole system is heated, the apparent weight of the sphere increases because
o: The metal expands more than the liquid, so the upthrust rises
The liquid expands more than the metal, so the upthrust falls
The mass of the sphere increases on heating
The density of the liquid increases on heating
questions.x: Upthrust = V_sphere × ρ_liquid × g. Liquids expand far more than metals, so ρ_liquid falls faster than V grows: upthrust drops, apparent weight rises.

questions.q: Water has its maximum density at
questions.x: Anomalous expansion: water contracts from 0°C to 4°C and expands above 4°C, so density peaks at 4°C.
questions.trap: 0°C: ice floats, but liquid water is densest at 4°C.

questions.q: A metal plate with a circular hole in it is heated. The hole
questions.x: Every linear dimension, including the hole's diameter, expands in proportion: the hole grows as if it were made of the metal.
questions.trap: 'Smaller': imagining the metal expands into the hole.

questions.q: The coefficient of real expansion of a liquid equals
o: Coefficient of apparent expansion − coefficient of cubical expansion of the vessel
Coefficient of apparent expansion × coefficient of cubical expansion of the vessel
Coefficient of apparent expansion + coefficient of cubical expansion of the vessel
questions.x: The vessel also expands, hiding part of the liquid's expansion: γ_real = γ_apparent + γ_vessel.

questions.q: A steel rod 1 m long (α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ /°C) is heated from 20°C to 120°C. Its length increases by
The triple point of water, where ice, water and vapour coexist, is at
questions.x: The triple point is 273.16 K (0.01°C, about 611 Pa). 273.15 K is 0°C, the ordinary melting point.
questions.trap: 273.15 K: that is 0°C, 0.01 K below the triple point.

questions.q: The heat needed to raise 2 kg of water from 20°C to 70°C is (c = 4200 J/kg K)
The heat capacity of a body is the heat needed to
o: Raise the temperature of 1 kg of it by 1 K
Melt the whole body at its melting point
Raise the temperature of the whole body by 1 K
Raise the temperature of an equal mass of water by 1 K
questions.x: Heat capacity = mc (J/K) refers to the whole body; specific heat capacity refers to unit mass.
questions.trap: '1 kg by 1 K' defines specific heat capacity.

questions.q: 10 g of ice at 0°C is mixed with 10 g of water at 80°C. The final temperature is (L = 336 J/g, c = 4.2 J/g°C)
questions.x: Melting all the ice needs 10 × 336 = 3360 J; water cooling 80→0°C gives 10 × 4.2 × 80 = 3360 J. All ice just melts; mixture at 0°C.
questions.trap: 40°C: averaging the temperatures and ignoring latent heat.

questions.q: A scald from steam at 100°C is more severe than one from water at 100°C because
o: Steam gives out its latent heat of vaporisation when it condenses on the skin
Steam is at a higher temperature than the water
Steam has a lower specific heat capacity
Steam conducts heat better than water
questions.x: Each gram of condensing steam releases about 2260 J before it even starts cooling as water.

questions.q: Food cooks faster in a pressure cooker because
o: The increased pressure lowers the boiling point of water
Steam carries less latent heat at high pressure
The cooker reduces the specific heat of food
The increased pressure raises the boiling point of water
questions.x: Boiling point rises with pressure (about 120°C inside a cooker), so food is cooked at a higher temperature.

questions.q: A 100 g calorimeter is made of a material of specific heat 0.84 J/g°C. Its water equivalent is (c_water = 4.2 J/g°C)
questions.x: Water equivalent = mc/c_w = 100 × 0.84/4.2 = 20 g.

questions.q: The zeroth law of thermodynamics leads to the concept of
questions.x: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, they are with each other: they share a common property, temperature.
questions.trap: Internal energy comes from the first law; entropy from the second.

questions.q: Heat flows through a rod at rate H. If both its length and its cross-sectional area are doubled (same material, same end temperatures), the rate becomes
questions.x: H = KAΔθ/L; doubling A and L leaves A/L, and hence H, unchanged.

questions.q: Two black bodies are at 300 K and 600 K. The ratio of energy each radiates per unit area per second is
questions.x: Stefan's law E = σT⁴: (300/600)⁴ = 1/16.
questions.trap: 1 : 2: using E ∝ T.

questions.q: By Stefan–Boltzmann law, the total energy radiated per second per unit area by a black body is proportional to
questions.x: E = σT⁴ with T in kelvin; σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

questions.q: The most suitable instrument for measuring the temperature of a furnace at about 2000°C is
questions.x: A radiation thermometer reads the radiation emitted, needing no contact, so it works far above the range of liquid-in-glass thermometers.

questions.q: A mercury-in-glass thermometer cannot be used to measure
o: The boiling point of water at 1 atm
questions.x: Mercury freezes at about −39°C; below that an alcohol or resistance thermometer is used.

questions.q: A platinum resistance thermometer works on the principle that
o: A heated junction of two metals produces an emf
A hot body emits radiation proportional to T⁴
The electrical resistance of a metal changes with temperature
questions.x: R_θ = R₀(1 + αθ); measuring R gives θ. The emf principle is the thermocouple; T⁴ is the radiation thermometer.

questions.q: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth by
questions.x: Space is nearly a vacuum; only radiation (electromagnetic waves) needs no medium.

questions.q: If the power radiated by a black body becomes 81 times, its absolute temperature becomes
questions.trap: 9 times: taking the square root instead of the fourth root.

questions.q: A temperature rise of 10°C is equal to a rise on the Fahrenheit scale of
questions.x: One Celsius degree = 9/5 Fahrenheit degrees, so 10 × 9/5 = 18°F. The +32 applies to readings, not differences.
questions.trap: 50°F: converting the reading 10°C, not the difference.

questions.q: The average translational kinetic energy of an ideal-gas molecule at absolute temperature T is
questions.x: Kinetic theory: ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT per molecule; (3/2)RT is per mole.
questions.trap: (3/2)RT is per mole, not per molecule.

questions.q: At the same temperature, the rms speeds of hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂) molecules are in the ratio
questions.trap: 16 : 1: forgetting the square root.

questions.q: The pressure of an ideal gas of density ρ whose molecules have rms speed c is
questions.x: Kinetic theory: P = ⅓ρc².

questions.q: The rms speed of gas molecules at 27°C is v. It becomes 2v at
questions.x: v ∝ √T, so T must become 4 × 300 K = 1200 K = 927°C.
questions.trap: 327°C (600 K): doubling T instead of making it four times; 1200°C forgets to convert from kelvin.

questions.q: At constant temperature, 6 L of a gas at 2 atm is compressed to 3 L. Its new pressure is
questions.x: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so P₂ = 2 × 6/3 = 4 atm.

questions.q: At the same temperature, the average translational kinetic energy per molecule of different ideal gases is
questions.x: Mean KE = (3/2)kT depends only on T. Lighter molecules move faster, but their KE is the same.
questions.trap: 'Lighter molecules': confusing KE with rms speed.

questions.q: In an isochoric (constant-volume) process, the work done by the gas is
questions.x: W = PΔV and ΔV = 0, so W = 0; all heat goes to internal energy.
questions.trap: 'Equal to the heat supplied': true of an isothermal process, not isochoric.

questions.q: When an ideal gas expands adiabatically, its temperature
o: Falls, because the work is done at the expense of internal energy
Stays constant, because no heat enters
questions.x: Q = 0, so ΔU = −W; positive work by the gas lowers U and hence T.
questions.trap: 'Stays constant': mixing up adiabatic (Q = 0) with isothermal (ΔT = 0).

questions.q: For one mole of an ideal gas, Mayer's relation is
questions.x: At constant pressure extra heat does work PΔV = RΔT, so Cp exceeds Cv by R.

questions.q: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 2 × 10⁵ Pa from 1 L to 3 L. The work done by the gas is
questions.trap: 4 × 10⁵ J: forgetting 1 L = 10⁻³ m³.

questions.q: 100 J of heat is supplied to a gas, which does 40 J of work. The change in its internal energy is
questions.x: First law: ΔU = Q − W = 100 − 40 = 60 J.

questions.q: A monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its volume. Its pressure becomes
questions.x: PV^γ = constant: P₂/P₁ = 8^(5/3) = 2⁵ = 32.
questions.trap: 8 times: applying Boyle's law to an adiabatic change.

questions.q: On a P–V diagram, at the same point the slope of an adiabatic curve is
o: Equal to the slope of the isothermal
1/γ times the slope of the isothermal
γ times the slope of the isothermal
questions.x: Isothermal dP/dV = −P/V; adiabatic dP/dV = −γP/V. Since γ > 1, the adiabatic is steeper.

questions.q: In a complete cyclic process, the change in internal energy of the system is
questions.x: Internal energy is a state function; the system returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W.

questions.q: The coefficient of performance of a Carnot refrigerator working between 270 K and 300 K is
questions.x: COP = T_cold/(T_hot − T_cold) = 270/30 = 9.
questions.trap: 10: using T_hot/(T_hot − T_cold), which is for a heat pump.

questions.q: In an irreversible process taking place in an isolated system, the total entropy
questions.x: Second law: entropy of an isolated system never decreases; it stays constant only for reversible processes.

questions.q: The efficiency of a Carnot engine could be 100% only if
o: Source and sink were at the same temperature
The working substance were an ideal gas
questions.x: η = 1 − T₂/T₁ = 1 only when T₂ = 0 K, which cannot be reached.

questions.q: In a four-stroke petrol engine, useful work is done on the piston during the
questions.x: The spark ignites the compressed mixture; the hot gas expands and pushes the piston in the power stroke.

questions.q: The Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law says that
o: Heat flows spontaneously from cold to hot bodies
No engine working in a cycle can convert all the heat it absorbs into work
Energy can be neither created nor destroyed
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature
questions.x: Some heat must always be rejected to a sink. 'Energy conserved' is the first law.

questions.q: A Carnot engine has an efficiency of 25% with its sink at 27°C. The temperature of its source is
questions.trap: 400°C: forgetting to convert 400 K to Celsius.

questions.q: 1 kg of ice melts at 0°C (L = 3.36 × 10⁵ J/kg). The change in its entropy is about
questions.x: ΔS = Q/T = 3.36 × 10⁵/273 ≈ 1231 J/K (T in kelvin).
questions.trap: 3.36 × 10⁵ J/K: forgetting to divide by the absolute temperature.

questions.q: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels at 340 m/s. Its wavelength is
Laplace corrected Newton's formula for the speed of sound in air by assuming that sound propagates
questions.x: Compressions and rarefactions are too fast for heat exchange, so the process is adiabatic: v = √(γP/ρ).
questions.trap: Isothermally: that was Newton's assumption, which gave about 280 m/s.

questions.q: The speed of sound in air is 332 m/s at 0°C. At 273°C it is about
questions.x: v ∝ √T: T doubles from 273 K to 546 K, so v = 332√2 ≈ 470 m/s.
questions.trap: 664 m/s: treating v ∝ T.

questions.q: Sound travels fastest in
questions.x: Speed is greatest in solids (high elasticity), then liquids, then gases; sound cannot travel in a vacuum.

questions.q: At constant temperature, the speed of sound in a gas is unaffected by a change in its
questions.x: v = √(γP/ρ); at constant T, P/ρ stays constant, so changing pressure changes nothing.
questions.trap: Humidity does change it: moist air is less dense, so sound is faster.

questions.q: Two points on a progressive wave are a quarter of a wavelength apart. Their phase difference is
questions.x: Phase difference = (2π/λ) × path difference = (2π/λ)(λ/4) = π/2.

questions.q: A progressive wave is y = 0.02 sin(100πt − 0.5πx) in SI units. Its speed is
In a stationary wave, the distance between two consecutive nodes is
questions.x: Nodes repeat every half wavelength; a node and the next antinode are λ/4 apart.
questions.trap: λ/4 is node-to-antinode.

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end can produce
questions.x: Closed end is a node, open end an antinode: f = nv/4L with n = 1, 3, 5, … An open pipe gives all harmonics.

questions.q: The fundamental frequency of an open pipe is 200 Hz. If one end is closed, the fundamental becomes
questions.x: Open: v/2L; closed: v/4L, half as much: 100 Hz.
questions.trap: 400 Hz: thinking closing the pipe raises pitch.

questions.q: The first overtone of an open pipe 50 cm long is (speed of sound 340 m/s)
questions.x: Fundamental v/2L = 340/1 = 340 Hz; first overtone = second harmonic = 680 Hz.
questions.trap: 340 Hz is the fundamental, not the first overtone.

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic. The number of nodes, including the two ends, is
questions.x: Third harmonic has 3 loops; n loops need n + 1 nodes = 4.

questions.q: A string has tension 100 N and mass per unit length 0.01 kg/m. The speed of transverse waves on it is
questions.trap: 10⁴ m/s: forgetting the square root.

questions.q: A car moving at 20 m/s towards a cliff sounds its 500 Hz horn. The frequency of the echo heard by the driver is (speed of sound 340 m/s)
questions.x: Cliff acts as a source receiving and re-emitting; driver is both moving source and observer: f' = f(v + u)/(v − u) = 500 × 360/320 = 562.5 Hz.
questions.trap: 531 Hz: applying only one Doppler shift.

questions.q: An observer moves at 34 m/s towards a stationary source of 400 Hz. The frequency heard is (speed of sound 340 m/s)
questions.x: Observer approaching: f' = f(v + v₀)/v = 400 × 374/340 = 440 Hz.
questions.trap: 444 Hz uses the moving-source formula v/(v − v₀).

questions.q: In still air, there is NO change in the observed frequency when
o: The source moves towards a stationary observer
The observer moves away from a stationary source
Source and observer move towards each other
Source and observer move in the same direction with the same velocity
questions.x: With no relative motion between source and observer (and still air), f' = f(v − u)/(v − u) = f.

questions.q: The pitch of a sound depends mainly on its
questions.x: Higher frequency gives higher pitch. Loudness depends on amplitude/intensity.
questions.trap: Amplitude decides loudness, not pitch.

questions.q: The quality (timbre) of a musical note depends on
o: The number and relative intensities of its overtones
The speed of sound in air
questions.x: Two instruments playing the same pitch and loudness differ in the overtones present; that gives quality.

questions.q: If the intensity of a sound increases 100 times, its intensity level increases by
questions.x: ΔL = 10 log₁₀(I₂/I₁) = 10 log₁₀100 = 20 dB.

questions.q: Two sound waves of the same frequency have amplitudes in the ratio 1 : 2. Their intensities are in the ratio
questions.x: Intensity ∝ (amplitude)²: (1/2)² = 1/4.
questions.trap: 1 : 2: taking I ∝ A.

questions.q: Two coherent waves with intensities in the ratio 9 : 1 interfere. The ratio of maximum to minimum intensity is
questions.x: Amplitude ratio = √9 : 1 = 3 : 1. I_max/I_min = (3 + 1)²/(3 − 1)² = 16/4 = 4.
questions.trap: 9 : 1: using the intensity ratio directly.

questions.q: Two light sources are coherent when they have
o: The same frequency and a constant phase difference
questions.x: Sustained interference needs a fixed phase relation; equal amplitude only improves contrast.

questions.q: A Young's double-slit apparatus is moved from air into water (refractive index 4/3). The fringe width
o: Becomes three-quarters of its value in air
Becomes four-thirds of its value in air
questions.x: β = λD/d and λ in water = λ/n, so β becomes β/(4/3) = 3β/4.
questions.trap: Four-thirds: multiplying by n instead of dividing.

questions.q: In an interference pattern, a dark fringe occurs where the path difference is
questions.x: Destructive interference: path difference = (2n + 1)λ/2, so waves meet out of phase.
questions.trap: Whole multiples of λ give bright fringes.

questions.q: In Young's double-slit experiment, the slit separation is halved and the slit–screen distance doubled. The fringe width becomes
questions.x: β = λD/d: D × 2 and d ÷ 2 give β × 4.

questions.q: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image is formed
o: 30 cm in front of the mirror
6 cm in front of the mirror
questions.x: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f (real positive): 1/v = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30, v = 30 cm, real, in front.
questions.trap: 6 cm comes from adding 1/10 + 1/15.

questions.q: For a real object, a convex mirror always forms an image that is
questions.x: A diverging mirror gives a virtual, upright, smaller image behind it for any object position (hence rear-view mirrors).

questions.q: A coin lies at the bottom of a tank of water 12 cm deep (refractive index 4/3). Seen from directly above, it appears raised by
questions.x: Apparent depth = 12/(4/3) = 9 cm, so the coin appears raised by 12 − 9 = 3 cm.
questions.trap: 9 cm is the apparent depth, not the rise.

questions.q: A vessel holds 8 cm of water (n = 4/3) with a 6 cm layer of an immiscible liquid (n = 1.5) floating on it. Viewed from directly above, a mark on the bottom appears to be below the top surface by
questions.x: Apparent depth = Σ tᵢ/nᵢ = 6/1.5 + 8/(4/3) = 4 + 6 = 10 cm.
questions.trap: 14 cm is the real depth.

questions.q: The refractive index of a given piece of glass does NOT depend on
questions.x: n = sin i / sin r stays the same for every angle of incidence; it does change with wavelength (dispersion), material and temperature.

questions.q: When light passes from air into glass, the quantity that does NOT change is its
questions.x: Frequency is fixed by the source; speed and wavelength both fall by the factor n.

questions.q: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels
o: From air to glass at any angle
From glass to air at an angle smaller than the critical angle
From air to water at an angle greater than 45°
From glass to air at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
questions.x: TIR needs denser → rarer medium and i > C.

questions.q: An equiconvex lens of glass (n = 1.5) has both radii of curvature 20 cm. Its power is
questions.trap: +0.05 D: leaving f in centimetres.

questions.q: A convex glass lens (n = 1.5) has focal length 20 cm in air. Immersed in water (n = 4/3), its focal length becomes
questions.trap: 26.7 cm: multiplying by n_water instead of using the lens maker's formula.

questions.q: The dispersive power of a transparent material is
questions.x: ω = angular dispersion/mean deviation = (n_v − n_r)/(n_y − 1); a dimensionless ratio.

questions.q: Two thin lenses of dispersive powers ω₁, ω₂ and focal lengths f₁, f₂ in contact form an achromatic combination when
questions.x: Achromatism needs zero change of combined power with colour: ω₁P₁ + ω₂P₂ = 0, i.e. ω₁/f₁ + ω₂/f₂ = 0 (one lens convex, one concave).

questions.q: Chromatic aberration in a lens is caused by
o: Rays far from the axis focusing differently from rays near it
The refractive index, and so the focal length, being different for different colours
questions.x: n depends on wavelength, so violet focuses closer than red. Marginal vs paraxial focusing is spherical aberration.
questions.trap: Marginal-ray focusing describes spherical aberration.

questions.q: The Sun looks reddish at sunrise and sunset mainly because
o: Red light is refracted more than blue light
Blue light is scattered out more along the long path through the atmosphere
The Sun is cooler in the morning and evening
The atmosphere absorbs red light less than it emits it
questions.x: Scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴; at low Sun the path is long, blue is scattered away, and the transmitted light is red-rich.

questions.q: In single-slit diffraction with slit width a, the first minimum lies at angle θ given by
questions.x: The slit splits into two halves whose wavelets cancel in pairs when a sinθ = λ.
questions.trap: λ/2: confusing it with the path difference for a dark fringe in double-slit interference.

questions.q: Diffraction of a wave is most noticeable when the size of the aperture or obstacle is
questions.x: Bending is significant only when the gap is of the order of λ; sound (long λ) diffracts round doors, light hardly does.

questions.q: A diffraction grating has 5000 lines per cm. For light of wavelength 500 nm, the first-order maximum occurs at sin θ =
questions.x: d = 1/5000 cm = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m; d sinθ = nλ gives sinθ = 5 × 10⁻⁷/2 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.25.

questions.q: The resolving power of a telescope can be increased by
o: Using an objective of smaller aperture
Using an objective of larger aperture
Using an eyepiece of longer focal length
questions.x: Resolving power ∝ D/λ (limit θ = 1.22λ/D): larger D or shorter λ.

questions.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through an ideal polaroid. The transmitted intensity is
questions.x: A polaroid passes only the component along its axis; averaging cos²θ over all directions gives ½.

questions.q: When light falls on glass at the Brewster (polarising) angle, the reflected and refracted rays are
questions.x: Brewster's law tan θp = n implies θp + r = 90°, so the rays are at 90°; the reflected ray is completely plane-polarised.

questions.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through two ideal polaroids whose axes are at 60°. The emerging intensity is
questions.x: First polaroid: I₀/2. Malus: (I₀/2)cos²60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8.
questions.trap: I₀/4: forgetting the first polaroid halves unpolarised light.

questions.q: A spring of force constant 200 N/m stores 0.25 J of elastic potential energy. Its extension is
questions.trap: 0.25 cm: computing 2U/k and forgetting the square root.

questions.q: In single-slit diffraction, the intensity of the first secondary maximum compared with the central maximum is about
questions.x: Secondary maxima fall off fast: I₁/I₀ ≈ 4/(9π²) ≈ 0.045, and the next ≈ 4/(25π²) ≈ 0.016. Almost all light is in the central band.
questions.trap: 50%: assuming all bright fringes are similar, as in double-slit interference.

questions.q: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm, 10 cm apart. For the final image at infinity (relaxed eye), the object must be placed from the objective at
questions.x: Final image at infinity: the objective's image lies at the eyepiece focus, so v = 10 − 5 = 5 cm. 1/u = 1/5 − 1/1 gives u = −1.25 cm.
questions.trap: 1.11 cm: taking the objective's image distance as the full 10 cm separation.

questions.q: Arranged in increasing order of size, the energy units are
questions.x: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, 1 erg = 10⁻⁷ J, 1 cal ≈ 4.2 J. So eV < erg < J < cal.
questions.trap: Placing the calorie below the joule; 1 calorie is about 4.2 J.

questions.q: A steel measuring tape is correct at 30°C. Used at 10°C, it reads exactly 50.00 cm for a rod. The true length of the rod is
o: Impossible to compare without the rod's α
questions.x: At 10°C the tape has contracted, so each marked centimetre is shorter than a true centimetre. 50 shrunken marks cover less than 50 true cm.
questions.trap: Thinking a contracted tape reads low; it actually reads high.

questions.q: An object moves towards a plane mirror with speed v along a line making angle θ with the normal. The speed of its image relative to the object is
questions.x: The component along the mirror (v sin θ) is the same for object and image; the normal component v cos θ is reversed. Relative velocity = 2v cos θ.
questions.trap: 2v: doubling the full speed instead of only the normal component.

questions.q: If the Earth began to spin faster about its axis, the weight of a body at the equator would
questions.x: Effective g = g − ω²R cos²λ. At the equator (λ = 0) a larger ω takes more of g for the centripetal force, so the weight falls. At the poles it is unchanged.
questions.trap: Remain unchanged: true only at the poles.

questions.q: The handle of a door is fixed at the edge farthest from the hinges so that
o: A small torque produces a large force
The door gains more linear momentum
A small force produces a large torque
The door's moment of inertia is reduced
questions.x: Torque τ = r × F. The largest perpendicular distance r from the hinge axis gives the needed turning effect with the least force.

questions.q: Two cars of masses M₁ and M₂ go round circular tracks of radii r₁ and r₂, each completing one round in the same time. The ratio of their angular speeds ω₁ : ω₂ is
questions.x: ω = 2π/T depends only on the time period. Equal periods give equal angular speeds, whatever the masses or radii.
questions.trap: r₁ : r₂ confuses angular speed with linear speed v = ωr.

questions.q: A thin disc of radius R has a central hole of radius r. It rests flat on a liquid of surface tension T. The total surface tension force on it is
questions.x: The liquid surface touches the disc along two edges: the outer rim (2πR) and the rim of the hole (2πr). F = T × total length = 2πT(R + r).
questions.trap: 2πT(R − r): subtracting the hole's edge instead of adding it.

questions.q: A boat of mass 1 × 10⁷ kg, initially at rest, is pushed by a constant net force of 5 × 10⁴ N through 4 m. Its speed then is
questions.x: Work–energy theorem: Fs = ½mv², so v = √(2Fs/m) = √(2 × 5 × 10⁴ × 4/10⁷) = √0.04 = 0.2 m/s.
questions.trap: 0.04 m/s is v², not v.

questions.q: As the temperature of a liquid rises, its surface tension
questions.x: Molecular cohesion weakens on heating, so surface tension falls, becoming zero at the critical temperature. Hot water cleans better for this reason.

questions.q: At a depth d below the Earth's surface, g falls to one-third of its surface value. Taking the Earth's radius as R, d equals
questions.x: Inside the Earth g_d = g(1 − d/R). Setting 1 − d/R = 1/3 gives d = 2R/3.
questions.trap: (√3 − 1)R is the height (not depth) where g becomes g/3.

questions.q: The first law of thermodynamics, dQ = dU + dW, is a statement of the conservation of
questions.x: Heat supplied goes partly into internal energy and partly into work done: no energy is created or lost.

questions.q: Three students measure g as 7.12, 7.13 and 7.12 m/s². These readings are
questions.x: The values agree closely with each other (precise) but are far from the true 9.8 m/s² (not accurate), pointing to a systematic error.
questions.trap: Close agreement among readings shows precision, not accuracy.

questions.q: A body of mass m moves on a string in a vertical circle of radius r. Its kinetic energy at the lowest point exceeds that at the highest point by
questions.x: Between top and bottom the body falls through the diameter 2r, so by energy conservation ΔKE = mg(2r) = 2mgr. Also v_bottom² − v_top² = 4gr.
questions.trap: 4mgr: forgetting the ½ in ½m(v_bottom² − v_top²).

questions.q: When a metal disc is heated, its moment of inertia about its own axis
questions.x: Expansion increases the radius while the mass stays the same, and I = ½MR², so I increases (and ω falls if it is spinning freely).

questions.q: A particle in SHM of amplitude A and period T starts from the mean position. The least time to reach x = A/2 is
questions.x: x = A sin(2πt/T). A/2 = A sin(2πt/T) gives 2πt/T = π/6, so t = T/12.
questions.trap: T/6 is the time from the extreme position to A/2.

questions.q: When an observer moves towards a stationary source of sound in still air, the observed frequency rises because
o: The wavelength of the sound decreases
The speed of sound in air increases
The speed of the waves relative to the observer increases
questions.x: The wavelength is unchanged (the source is still). Moving towards it, the observer meets more wavefronts per second: f' = (v + v₀)/λ.
questions.trap: Wavelength changes only when the source moves.

questions.q: The width of a notebook is measured with a metre scale having millimetre divisions. The correctly recorded reading is
questions.x: Least count 1 mm = 0.1 cm, so the reading is recorded to one decimal place in cm. 21 cm drops a significant figure; 21.03 cm claims precision the scale lacks.
questions.trap: 21 cm looks equal but hides the 0.1 cm precision.

questions.q: For measuring temperatures below 1 K, the thermometer generally used is the
questions.x: A magnetic thermometer uses the susceptibility of a paramagnetic salt (Curie's law, χ ∝ 1/T), which works at very low temperatures. Pyrometers are for very high ones.

questions.q: The dimensional formula of surface tension is
questions.x: Surface tension = force/length = [MLT⁻²]/[L] = [MT⁻²]. [ML⁻¹T⁻²] is pressure.
questions.trap: [ML⁻¹T⁻²] is the formula for pressure or stress.

questions.q: The product 2.5 × 1.25, written to the correct number of significant figures, is
questions.x: In multiplication the answer keeps as many significant figures as the least precise factor: 2.5 has two, so 3.125 → 3.1.
questions.trap: 3.13 keeps three figures, set by 1.25 instead of 2.5.

questions.q: In the relation F = ax + bt², F is force, x is displacement and t is time. The dimensions of a/b are
questions.x: a = F/x = [MT⁻²]; b = F/t² = [MLT⁻⁴]. a/b = [MT⁻²]/[MLT⁻⁴] = [L⁻¹T²].

questions.q: Two forces of 5 N and 3 N act at a point in any directions. Their resultant can NOT be
questions.x: The resultant lies between the difference and the sum: 5 − 3 = 2 N to 5 + 3 = 8 N. 1 N is outside this range.
questions.trap: 2 N looks too small, but it is the minimum, with the forces opposite.

questions.q: The area under a velocity–time graph gives the
questions.x: Area = ∫v dt = displacement. The slope of the v–t graph gives acceleration.
questions.trap: Acceleration is the slope, not the area.

questions.q: A body starts from rest with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s². The distance it covers in the 5th second is
questions.x: sₙ = u + a(2n − 1)/2 = 0 + 2 × 9/2 = 9 m. (25 m is the total in 5 s; 16 m in 4 s.)
questions.trap: 25 m is the distance covered in all five seconds.

questions.q: A projectile is launched at 45° to the horizontal. The ratio of its horizontal range to its maximum height is
questions.x: R = u² sin 2θ/g = u²/g; H = u² sin²θ/2g = u²/4g. So R/H = 4. In general R = 4H/tan θ.

questions.q: A ball is projected at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Its time of flight is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.trap: 4 s uses u instead of u sin θ.

questions.q: Two trains move towards each other on parallel tracks at 54 km/h and 36 km/h. The speed of one relative to the other is
questions.x: Moving towards each other, relative speed = 54 + 36 = 90 km/h = 90/3.6 = 25 m/s.
questions.trap: 5 m/s subtracts the speeds, which applies to the same direction.

questions.q: A stone is dropped from rest from a height of 80 m. The time it takes to fall the last 35 m is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.x: Total time: 80 = 5t², t = 4 s. Time to fall the first 45 m: 45 = 5t², t = 3 s. Last 35 m takes 4 − 3 = 1 s.

questions.q: The area under a force–time graph gives the
questions.x: Impulse = ∫F dt = Δp. The area under a force–displacement graph would give work.
questions.trap: Work is the area under force–displacement, not force–time.

questions.q: A car moves at a steady 20 m/s against total resistive forces of 500 N. The power delivered by its engine is
questions.x: At steady speed the driving force equals the resistance. P = Fv = 500 × 20 = 10 000 W = 10 kW.

questions.q: A 10 kg block on a rough horizontal floor (μ_k = 0.2) is pulled by a horizontal force of 50 N. Its acceleration is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.x: Friction = μmg = 0.2 × 10 × 10 = 20 N. Net force 50 − 20 = 30 N, a = 30/10 = 3 m/s².
questions.trap: 5 m/s² ignores friction.

questions.q: A bomb of mass 3 kg at rest explodes into two pieces of 1 kg and 2 kg. The 1 kg piece moves at 20 m/s. The total kinetic energy produced is
questions.trap: 200 J counts only the lighter piece.

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a rigid body does NOT depend on its
o: Distribution of mass about the axis
Position of the axis of rotation
questions.x: I = Σmr² depends on the mass and how far it lies from the chosen axis, not on how fast the body turns.

questions.q: In rotational motion, the quantity that plays the role that mass plays in linear motion is
questions.x: Moment of inertia measures resistance to change in rotational motion, as mass measures resistance to change in linear motion (τ = Iα vs F = ma).
questions.trap: Torque is the analogue of force, not mass.

questions.q: The ratio of the moment of inertia of a uniform rod about a perpendicular axis through one end to that about a parallel axis through its centre is
questions.x: I_end = ML²/3 and I_centre = ML²/12. Ratio = (1/3)/(1/12) = 4.

questions.q: A uniform rod of mass 3 kg and length 2 m is free to turn about a perpendicular axis through its centre. A torque of 2 N m gives it an angular acceleration of
questions.x: I = ML²/12 = 3 × 4/12 = 1 kg m². α = τ/I = 2/1 = 2 rad/s².
questions.trap: 0.5 rad/s² uses I = ML²/3 about the end.

questions.q: A constant torque of 5 N m turns a wheel through 2 complete revolutions. The work done by the torque is about
questions.x: W = τθ with θ in radians: 2 revolutions = 4π rad. W = 5 × 4π ≈ 62.8 J.
questions.trap: 10 J uses θ = 2 instead of 4π radians.

questions.q: If the Earth contracted to half its present radius with no change in mass, the length of a day would become
questions.x: Angular momentum Iω is conserved and I ∝ R². Halving R makes I one-fourth, so ω becomes 4 times and the day 24/4 = 6 h.
questions.trap: 12 hours takes I ∝ R instead of R².

questions.q: The orbital speed of a satellite moving just above the Earth's surface is about
questions.x: v₀ = √(gR) = √(9.8 × 6.4 × 10⁶) ≈ 7.9 km/s. 11.2 km/s (√2 times larger) is the escape velocity.
questions.trap: 11.2 km/s is the escape velocity.

questions.q: Taking the gravitational potential energy as zero at infinity, a mass m at a height equal to the Earth's radius R above the surface has potential energy
questions.x: U = −GMm/r with r measured from the Earth's centre: r = R + R = 2R, so U = −GMm/2R.
questions.trap: −GMm/4R uses r² as for force or field.

questions.q: The period of revolution of a geostationary satellite is
questions.x: It turns with the Earth, west to east in the equatorial plane, so it stays above one point; its period equals the Earth's rotation period.

questions.q: An astronaut inside a satellite orbiting the Earth feels weightless because
o: There is no gravity at that height
Both the astronaut and the satellite are falling freely with the same acceleration
The Moon's pull cancels the Earth's pull
The satellite is outside the atmosphere
questions.x: Gravity there is still strong (g only slightly less). Both fall towards the Earth with the same acceleration, so the floor pushes nothing on the astronaut.
questions.trap: Gravity does not vanish at orbital height; g is still about 90% of its surface value in low orbit.

questions.q: A planet has twice the mass and twice the radius of the Earth. The acceleration due to gravity on its surface is (g = Earth's value)
questions.x: g = GM/R². Mass ×2, R² ×4: g' = 2/4 × g = g/2.
questions.trap: g forgets that the radius enters squared.

questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity at the centre of the Earth is
questions.x: At depth d, g' = g(1 − d/R). At the centre d = R, so g' = 0: the pulls of the surrounding mass cancel.

questions.q: A body moves in a circle of radius 5 m at a steady speed of 10 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is
questions.x: a = v²/r = 100/5 = 20 m/s², directed towards the centre.
questions.trap: 0: the speed is constant, but the direction keeps changing.

questions.q: A curved road of radius 40 m is to be banked so that a car at 20 m/s needs no friction. The angle of banking is (g = 10 m/s²)
A 0.5 kg stone on a string moves in a vertical circle of radius 1 m. At the lowest point its speed is 4 m/s. The tension in the string there is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.x: At the bottom T − mg = mv²/r: T = 0.5 × 10 + 0.5 × 16/1 = 5 + 8 = 13 N.
questions.trap: 3 N subtracts the weight; at the bottom gravity adds to the needed tension.

questions.q: A particle executes SHM of amplitude A. When its displacement is A/2, the fraction of its total energy that is kinetic is
questions.x: PE = ½kx² = ¼ of ½kA² at x = A/2. KE = 1 − ¼ = ¾ of the total.
questions.trap: 1/4 is the potential energy fraction.

questions.q: The hydraulic lift and hydraulic brakes work on
questions.x: Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is passed equally to all parts, so a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston.

questions.q: The pressure due to water alone at a depth of 10 m in a lake is (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²)
questions.x: P = hρg = 10 × 1000 × 10 = 10⁵ Pa, about one atmosphere. Adding the air above gives about 2 × 10⁵ Pa in total.
questions.trap: 2 × 10⁵ Pa adds atmospheric pressure; the question asks for water alone.

questions.q: The excess pressure inside a small liquid drop of radius r and surface tension T is
questions.x: A drop has one free surface: ΔP = 2T/r. A soap bubble has two surfaces, giving 4T/r.
questions.trap: 4T/r is for a soap bubble with two surfaces.

questions.q: A glass capillary tube is dipped in water inside a satellite in orbit (weightless). The water
o: Rises to the same height as on Earth
Overflows from the top as a fountain
Rises to the top of the tube without overflowing
questions.x: With g effectively zero, nothing limits the rise (h ∝ 1/g), so water climbs to the end. There the meniscus adjusts its curvature, so it does not overflow.
questions.trap: Overflow never happens: the meniscus flattens at the top.

questions.q: Stress has the same dimensions as
questions.x: Stress = force/area, which is also the definition of pressure: [ML⁻¹T⁻²]. Strain is dimensionless.

questions.q: The only modulus of elasticity that liquids and gases possess is the
questions.x: Fluids cannot keep a fixed shape or length, so they have no Young's or shear modulus, but they resist compression.

questions.q: Poisson's ratio has
questions.x: It is lateral strain ÷ longitudinal strain, a ratio of two pure numbers.

questions.q: A wire stretches by 2 mm when a load of 100 N hangs from it. The elastic potential energy stored in it is
questions.x: U = ½ × F × extension = ½ × 100 × 0.002 = 0.1 J.
questions.trap: 0.2 J forgets the ½.

questions.q: A wire can bear a maximum load W before breaking. Another wire of the same material with twice the radius can bear
questions.x: Breaking stress is a property of the material. Breaking load = stress × area, and area ∝ r², so it becomes 4W.
questions.trap: 2W takes area ∝ r.

questions.q: A wire of cross-section 1 mm² and Young's modulus 2 × 10¹¹ N/m² carries a load of 200 N. The longitudinal strain is
questions.x: Stress = 200/10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁸ N/m². Strain = stress/Y = 2 × 10⁸/2 × 10¹¹ = 10⁻³.
questions.trap: 1 × 10⁻⁵ forgets to convert mm² to m².

questions.q: Mechanical transverse waves can NOT travel through
questions.x: Transverse waves need a restoring force against shear (rigidity). Gases have none, so sound in air is longitudinal only.

questions.q: The speed of sound in air at 0 °C is v. It becomes 2v at
questions.x: v ∝ √T. For 2v, T must be 4 × 273 = 1092 K = 819 °C.
questions.trap: 1092 is the answer in kelvin, not °C.

questions.q: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels at 350 m/s. Two points 35 cm apart along its path differ in phase by
At the same temperature and pressure, sound travels slightly faster in humid air than in dry air because humid air
questions.x: Water vapour (M = 18) is lighter than air (M ≈ 29), so humid air is less dense and v = √(γP/ρ) rises.
questions.trap: Many think moist air is heavier; water vapour is lighter than dry air.

questions.q: In a stationary wave, the distance between a node and the next antinode is
questions.x: Nodes are λ/2 apart and antinodes lie midway between them, so node to antinode is λ/4.
questions.trap: λ/2 is node to node.

questions.q: The frequencies of the first three harmonics of a pipe open at both ends are in the ratio
questions.x: An open pipe gives all harmonics: f, 2f, 3f. A closed pipe gives only odd ones: 1 : 3 : 5.
questions.trap: 1 : 3 : 5 is for a pipe closed at one end.

questions.q: A string 0.5 m long, fixed at both ends, carries transverse waves at 200 m/s. Its fundamental frequency is
questions.x: In the fundamental, L = λ/2, so λ = 1 m and f = v/λ = 200 Hz.
questions.trap: 400 Hz takes λ = L.

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end has length L. An open pipe with the same fundamental frequency must have length
questions.x: Closed: f = v/4L. Open: f = v/2L′. Equal when 2L′ = 4L, so L′ = 2L.
questions.trap: L/2 inverts the relation.

questions.q: The intensity of a sound is 10⁻⁶ W/m². Taking the threshold intensity as 10⁻¹² W/m², its intensity level is
questions.x: β = 10 log(I/I₀) = 10 log(10⁶) = 60 dB.
questions.trap: 6 dB forgets the factor 10 (that is in bels).

questions.q: The distance from a small source of sound is doubled. The intensity of the sound becomes
questions.x: A point source spreads its power over 4πr², so I ∝ 1/r².
questions.trap: Half takes I ∝ 1/r.

questions.q: A 500 Hz source moves away from a stationary observer at 30 m/s. The frequency heard is about (speed of sound 330 m/s)
questions.x: Source receding: f′ = f v/(v + v_s) = 500 × 330/360 ≈ 458 Hz.
questions.trap: 550 Hz uses the formula for an approaching source.

questions.q: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm. The image is
o: Real, 10 cm in front, half the size
Virtual, 10 cm behind the mirror, half the size
questions.x: Real-is-positive: f = −20 cm (convex), u = +20 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 − 1/20 = −1/10, so v = −10 cm (virtual, behind). m = −v/u = ½.
questions.trap: At infinity applies to an object at the focus of a concave mirror.

questions.q: A prism of angle 60° gives a minimum deviation of 30°. Its refractive index is
The interference of light gives evidence for its
questions.x: Only waves can add to give bright and dark fringes. Transverse nature is shown by polarisation, not interference.
questions.trap: Polarisation, not interference, shows light is transverse.

questions.q: In Young's double-slit experiment, at the centre of the third bright fringe (not counting the central one) the path difference is
questions.x: Bright fringes occur where path difference = nλ. For n = 3 it is 3λ. Odd multiples of λ/2 give dark fringes.
questions.trap: 5λ/2 is the condition for the third dark fringe.

questions.q: In Young's experiment, λ = 500 nm, slit separation 0.5 mm and screen distance 1 m. The distance of the second bright fringe from the centre is
questions.trap: 1 mm is one fringe width.

questions.q: If white light is used in Young's double-slit experiment, the central fringe is
o: White, with coloured fringes on both sides
questions.x: At the centre the path difference is zero for every colour, so all colours are bright together and give white. Elsewhere fringes of different λ separate.

questions.q: In Young's experiment the fringe width is 0.6 mm with light of 600 nm. Using 400 nm light, everything else unchanged, the fringe width becomes
questions.trap: 0.9 mm uses the inverse ratio.

questions.q: We can hear a person talking round the corner of a building but cannot see them, mainly because
o: Sound wavelengths are comparable to the size of the obstacle, light wavelengths are far smaller
Sound is reflected but light is not
questions.x: Diffraction is noticeable when the obstacle is comparable to the wavelength: sound ≈ 1 m, light ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁷ m.
questions.trap: Sound is far slower than light, not faster.

questions.q: The Brewster (polarising) angle for light reflected from water of refractive index 1.33 is about
questions.x: tan θp = n = 1.33, so θp ≈ 53°. The refracted ray then travels at 90° − 53° = 37° to the normal.
questions.trap: 37° is the angle of refraction at Brewster incidence.

questions.q: A copper rod (k = 400 W/m K) of length 0.5 m and cross-section 1 cm² has its ends at 100 °C and 0 °C. In steady state the rate of heat flow is
questions.trap: 80 W forgets 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², not 10⁻³ m².

questions.q: If α is the coefficient of linear expansion, the coefficient of superficial (area) expansion of the solid is
questions.x: Area involves two lengths: β = 2α. Volume involves three: γ = 3α.
questions.trap: 3α is the cubical coefficient.

questions.q: A bimetallic strip of brass and iron (α_brass > α_iron) is heated. It bends with
o: Brass on the inner side, then straightens
questions.x: Brass expands more, so it becomes the longer, outer side of the curve. This is used in thermostats and fire alarms.

questions.q: 1 L of a liquid with coefficient of cubical expansion 1 × 10⁻³ /°C is warmed by 50 °C. Its volume increases by about
questions.trap: 150 mL multiplies by 3, but γ is already the cubical coefficient.

questions.q: A pendulum clock with a metal pendulum rod keeps correct time at 20 °C. On a hot day it
o: Loses time, because the pendulum lengthens and its period increases
Gains time, because the pendulum lengthens
Gains time, because the period decreases
Keeps correct time, because g is unchanged
questions.x: T = 2π√(l/g). Expansion lengthens l, so each swing takes longer and the clock runs slow (loses time).
questions.trap: A longer period means fewer ticks per hour: the clock loses.

questions.q: Water is used as the coolant in car radiators mainly because it has a
questions.x: High c means each kilogram absorbs a lot of heat for a small rise in temperature.

questions.q: The heat released when 5 g of steam at 100 °C condenses to water at 100 °C is (latent heat of vaporisation = 2260 J/g)
questions.x: Q = mL = 5 × 2260 = 11 300 J; temperature does not change during condensation.

questions.q: The heat needed to change 10 g of ice at −10 °C into water at 0 °C is (c_ice = 2.1 J/g °C, L = 336 J/g)
questions.x: Warm the ice: 10 × 2.1 × 10 = 210 J. Melt it: 10 × 336 = 3360 J. Total 3570 J.
questions.trap: 3360 J forgets to warm the ice to 0 °C first.

questions.q: Water boils below 100 °C at the top of a high mountain because
o: The atmospheric pressure there is lower
The air there has less oxygen
questions.x: Water boils when its vapour pressure equals the outside pressure. Lower pressure is reached at a lower temperature.

questions.q: Boltzmann's constant k is related to the gas constant R and Avogadro's number N_A by
questions.x: k is the gas constant per molecule: 8.31/(6.02 × 10²³) ≈ 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.

questions.q: 2 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K occupy 0.0249 m³. Its pressure is (R = 8.3 J/mol K)
questions.trap: 1 × 10⁵ Pa forgets n = 2.

questions.q: For a diatomic ideal gas at room temperature, γ = Cp/Cv is
questions.x: Five degrees of freedom: Cv = 5R/2, Cp = 7R/2, γ = 1.4. 5/3 is for a monatomic gas.
questions.trap: 5/3 is the monatomic value.

questions.q: At constant temperature, the volume of a gas is reduced by 20%. Its pressure increases by
questions.x: Boyle: P₁V₁ = P₂(0.8V₁), so P₂ = 1.25P₁, an increase of 25%.
questions.trap: 20% assumes the changes are equal and opposite.

questions.q: When an ideal gas is heated at constant volume, all the heat supplied
o: Is shared equally between work and internal energy
questions.x: dW = PdV = 0 at constant volume, so by the first law dQ = dU.

questions.q: One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally to twice its volume. The work done by the gas is about (R = 8.31 J/mol K, ln 2 = 0.693)
questions.trap: 2493 J is nRT, forgetting the ln 2.

questions.q: Heat is supplied to a monatomic ideal gas at constant pressure. The fraction of this heat used in doing external work is
questions.x: Q = nCpΔT = (5/2)nRΔT; W = PΔV = nRΔT. W/Q = 1/(5/2) = 2/5. The other 3/5 raises the internal energy.
questions.trap: 3/5 is the fraction going into internal energy.

questions.q: The Clausius statement of the second law of thermodynamics says that
o: Heat cannot by itself flow from a colder body to a hotter one
Energy can be neither created nor destroyed
Two bodies in equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other
The entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero
questions.x: A refrigerator moves heat from cold to hot only because external work is supplied. The other options are the first, zeroth and third laws.

questions.q: The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends on
o: Only the temperatures of the source and the sink
questions.x: η = 1 − T₂/T₁. Any reversible engine between the same two temperatures has the same efficiency, whatever the working substance.

questions.q: A heat engine of efficiency 40% absorbs 500 J of heat from its source in each cycle. The heat it rejects to the sink per cycle is
questions.x: Work = 0.4 × 500 = 200 J. Heat rejected = 500 − 200 = 300 J.
questions.trap: 200 J is the work done, not the heat rejected.

questions.q: A refrigerator takes 300 J of heat from its cold interior using 100 J of electrical work. The heat it gives out to the room is
questions.x: Energy conservation: heat to room = heat taken + work done = 300 + 100 = 400 J. Its COP is 300/100 = 3.
questions.trap: 300 J forgets that the work also ends up as heat in the room.
